messages.mes:
The verge gave way to wheel ruts, and the ruts to a road wide enough for two carts abreast. Glassmere's walls stood a gray half-mile on, old stone patched with older stone, and the traffic thickened as the morning went: a boy driving geese with a switch, two carts of firewood, a woman with empty pails swinging at her hips. Sun climbed off the fields and the wind lost its edge.

The gate stood open. Foot traffic passed through a side arch with little more than a glance from the guards in the gatehouse shade; the carts queued longer, and a guard walked the line thumping sack tops with a stick. Inside the arch the air changed all at once — bread, horse, woodsmoke, the sour breath of a drain. Somewhere beyond the roofs lay water; gulls rode the updraft above the lanes.

Glassmere worked its morning. A smith's hammer kept a slow beat off a side court. A shop front near the first square showed a faceted stone painted in gold over the door, and two young people in gray hoods stood under it arguing over a ledger, the taller one jabbing a finger at a column of figures. Laundry crossed the narrow street overhead on a drooping line. Nobody looked at the staff in Alaric's hand longer than at anything else.

He found the Guild by its signboard, hung out over a cobbled square: a shield crossed by sword and staff, the words ADVENTURERS' GUILD beneath in plain black lettering. The hall behind it was wider than the shops around it, timber-framed over a stone ground floor, its doors standing open to the air.

From the threshold the room ran deep. A long counter held the near wall, a clerk behind it stamping a stack of slips with a wooden press, thump, thump. Notice boards crowded the far side, papers layered three deep. A man in scarred mail stood at the boards with his arms folded, reading. A woman in a stained apron swept the floor near the benches, pushing yesterday's mud toward a bucket.

The clerk reached the end of the stack and dipped the press again.

The clerk looked up from the stack, a thin man with ink on the side of his thumb and spectacles pushed up into his hair. The press came down on one more slip, thump, and then he set it aside.

"Registration. Two silver, one-time, and you're in the rolls for life." He turned sideways and took a slim ledger down from a shelf behind him without hurrying. "That covers your Guild Rank — you'd start Novice — the contract slips, the branch rolls everywhere, not just Glassmere. Any branch you walk into can find you in the book."

He laid the ledger open on the counter, still blank at the newest page, and squared it with two fingers.

"Understand the two scales, because people trip on it. Guild Rank is standing with us — what work you're allowed to take, Novice up to Legend. Power Rank is what you can actually do, F up to S. The stone measures the second. We record the first." He nodded at the open page. "Two silver, your name, and it's done. If you're wanting work today, the board's over there."

messages.mes:
The two silver crossed the counter with a small double click. The clerk swept them into a drawer, wrote *Alaric Red* into the ledger in a quick, slanted hand, and turned the book so the ink could catch the light from the window.

"Red. R-E-D?" He made the correction without waiting, then reached under the counter and brought up a wooden tray of thin metal plates, each stamped with the shield-and-staff. He chose one, inked the name beneath the mark with a fine brush, and dusted it with sand. "Hold that a moment."

He carried the plate to the end of the counter, where a dull crystal the size of a fist sat set into a wooden stand, and set Alaric's hand flat on it with the plate beneath. The crystal woke with a faint warmth under his palm and a low hum, flickered, and settled on a pale amber glow.

"F." The clerk noted it in the ledger. "That's your measured strength, nothing to do with us — the stone just reads it. We record you Novice. When the stone reads higher, come back and we'll move your standing up." He pressed the plate into Alaric's hand, cool metal, edges worn smooth by other hands before his. "That's yours. Show it to take contracts, show it at any branch. Board's over there if you want work today."

The press thumped down on a fresh slip behind him. At the boards, the man in scarred mail peeled a notice free and carried it toward the counter.

The clerk took the slip, glanced at the blue seal, and opened the ledger to the fresh page with Alaric's name on it.

"Glimmerdeep. Good first work." He wrote the contract title beneath the name, dated it, and pressed the wooden stamp down on the slip — thump — then turned it around so Alaric could read the ink. *ACTIVE*, in the Guild's block letters, under the shield-and-staff. "Keep that on you. When the work's done, bring it back to any desk and we close it out and pay you there — one hundred twenty copper, posted and guaranteed. The client doesn't pay you; we do."

He slid the slip across the counter.

"Now, Glimmerdeep you'll know or you won't, so — the cleft's a morning's walk north, where the stream comes out of the hills. Can't miss it once you're on the north road; the water runs bright. The academy holds the place. Outer galleries are yours to cull, the deep galleries are theirs — there's a sealed gate down level one and you'll want to leave it sealed. Beetles and slimes, nothing that's killed a Novice who kept his head. Slimes burn slow, beetles come at you straight." He picked up his next slip and squared it against the counter edge. messages.mes:
The north road left the city through the cattle gate and climbed gently between hedged fields, the morning still cool enough that his breath showed faintly. Carts and a knacker's dray passed him heading in; after the first mile the traffic thinned to a shepherd and her dog, and then to nobody. The stream kept him company more than the road did — visible now and then through gaps in the hedgerows, running quick and shallow over brown stones, exactly as the clerk had said it would.

By midmorning the fields gave out. The hedges ended at a drystone wall, and beyond it the ground rose into wooded hills, the road narrowing to a cart track that followed the water. The stream ran brighter here, tinted faintly green where the light caught it, and cold air breathed out of the shade of the trees. Twice the road crossed the stream on slab bridges worn slick at their edges.

The cleft announced itself before he saw it: a glimmering in the hillside, glimpsed through the trees, like light off water where there was no water. Then the track bent, and there it was — a split in the rock face perhaps thirty feet high, the stream sliding out of it over a lip of stone. Crystal grew along both walls of the opening in thick pale columns, catching the sun and throwing it back in slow shifting patches across the ground. A narrow path of packed earth ran alongside the water into the shadow, and just inside the mouth, where the daylight still reached, a wooden post stood with a painted board nailed to it.

The board read, in a careful academic hand: *Glimmerdeep — property of Lanternhall Academy. Outer galleries open to registered adventurers. The gate below remains sealed. Report damage or breach at the Academy.*

The stream's noise filled the cleft, and under it, faintly, came a sound from deeper in — a slow, dry scraping, like something dragging across stone.

messages.mes:
The path ran in beside the water, and the stream noise changed as the rock closed overhead — deeper, with an echo under it now. The daylight held for twenty paces, then gave way to the crystal's own light: pale columns growing from wall and floor and even the ceiling, glowing faintly from within, cool blue-white, bright enough to walk by. The air smelled of wet stone and something mineral and sweet, like rain on quartz.

The path climbed a little away from the water, turned past a knot of crystal that had grown right through the old trackbed, and opened into the first gallery — a low vault where the stream pooled and slid away through a gap too narrow for a person. Small glints studded the gravel near the waterline: flakes of loose crystal, free for the taking if a man wanted to stoop for them. Old bootprints crossed the sand at the gallery's edge, weeks old, softened at their edges. Nothing moved.

Beyond the pool the gallery narrowed, then stepped down through a crack in the rock into a second chamber, colder, the crystal here growing in tall sharp spires that ticked faintly against each other when the water beneath them shivered. His footsteps carried. Somewhere ahead the scraping sound came again — closer now, a dry chitin drag over stone, then a pause, then again.

He came around a spire the size of a fence post and found the source.

Two beetles worked at a fallen column of crystal in the middle of the chamber, their shells the same pale blue as the stone around them, so that at rest they would have been nearly invisible — but they were moving, mandibles rasping crystal flakes off the broken column, and the motion gave them away. Each was the size of a large dog, low and broad, legs planted wide. One stopped feeding. Its head came around, antennae tasting the air in his direction, and the second lifted its own head a heartbeat later.

The first beetle clicked its mandibles once and started toward him across the chamber floor, the other following at an angle, the pair of them opening out as they came.

The lance caught the beetle as it gathered itself to spring, fire punching through the pale shell at the shoulder joint. The creature heaved sideways, legs scraping at the gravel, mandibles working at nothing — then the light in the shell went out of it, faint as a lamp guttering, and it collapsed across the broken crystal column with a last dry ticking of legs.

Then the chamber was quiet. The stream ran on beneath the spires, and the crystal light steadied, blue-white and patient.

His forearm throbbed where the mandibles had crushed it, blood sticking his sleeve to the skin, but the beetle's venom had come with the bite and was already in his pouch — a gland the fight had left intact, slick and pale, settled among three chitin plates cracked loose from the shells. Neither corpse stirred. Both beetles lay still in the crystal glow, one smoking, one splayed across the broken column, and nothing else moved in the second chamber but the water.

Ahead, the chamber narrowed where the stream slid under a shelf of rock, and the crystal spires thinned toward a darker passage beyond.

messages.mes:
The tunnel took him down. The stream ran alongside under the shelf, faster now, and the crystal grew sparser along the walls — fewer columns, more raw stone furred with a thin mineral crust that glimmered only when his staff-light crossed it. The air cooled further. His boots splashed through shallow runs of water where the floor dipped, and once something small and blind fled ahead of his feet with a wet scrabble, gone before he could see what it was. Old claw-marks scored one wall at shoulder height, three parallel grooves, weeks or months old. Nothing made them now.

The passage turned, widened, and let out into a third gallery where the ceiling rose out of sight and the stream spread into a wide, glassy sheet across the floor, barely a finger deep.

The pool was not empty.

In the middle of it, half sunk like a mound of wet sand, sat a thing the size of a feed sack — translucent, milky, shot through with veins of the same pale crystal light as the walls. It did not move. The water around it lay perfectly still, without so much as a ripple from the thing's edge, and where its mass touched the gravel the pebbles showed through its body, blurred, as if seen through oiled cloth. The stream fed in from behind it and the water simply went under it, or through it, and came out the other side.

It might have been a rock formation. It might have been asleep.

His splash into the shallow water had already carried to it, ring after ring sliding across the still surface toward that milky edge — and as the first ring touched it, the whole mass shifted, a slow sliding pull of weight, and a corner of it lifted from the pool floor like a wave deciding which way to break.

messages.mes:
The lance struck the mound before it finished rising, fire punching into that translucent mass and blooming inside it like a lamp dropped in milk. A third of the thing simply went with the shot — a ragged patch of its body flash-boiled, sloughing away in a hiss of steam and settling into the shallow water as gritty white sediment. The veins of crystal light in it guttered, dimmed, and the whole mound convulsed.

Then it surged.

It came across the pool floor faster than something that shape had any right to move, a sliding wave of milky mass dragging itself over the gravel, and it reached him before he could back off the wet stone. The edge of it folded over his boot and ankle — and where it touched, his boot leather went soft, the lace stiffening, the skin beneath lighting up with a cold burning that was not heat at all. It ate at him the way water eats at limestone. He wrenched his foot free, and a patch of his boot sole came away grayed and pitted, thin as old paper.

The ooze pulled itself back together a pace away, half its former bulk, steaming faintly at the wound the lance had burned through its middle. The shallow water around it had gone cloudy with the grit of what it had lost. It gathered at its broken edge, weight shifting, the light in its veins pulsing slow — still coming, still hungry, but visibly less of it than there had been.

His ankle throbbed under the corroded leather, and the thing was already reaching for him again.

Then it was only water and powder, running off toward the stream's edge, and a residue of pale gel sitting in the wreck of it that settled into his pouch alongside the rest without a thought from him.

The gallery went quiet again. The shallow sheet of water cleared slowly as the sediment sank, rings still working their way outward from where the thing had stood, and the stream kept its unhurried course across the floor and out under the far wall. His boot was the worse for it — the sole thinned to gray leather near the toe, pitted like old bone, the skin beneath unbroken but tender through the gap.

The ceiling still rose away into dark above, and along the far side of the gallery the water ran out through a low gap in the rock, a gap wide enough to take a man crouched or walking bent, breathing cooler air out of whatever lay beyond. The way he had come stood open behind him. Nothing in the chamber moved but the water.

messages.mes:
The columns thinned and thickened without pattern, some leaning, some split down the middle like felled trees of glass, and he picked his way between them with his light held low. The floor told the story better than the ceiling did. Old channels scored the stone where water had run in some earlier age, and in the dried mud of one of them a track pressed clean and whole — the same ridged, clawed print the beetles had left back in the first gallery, but larger, and laid over another, and another, all bearing the same direction.

He gave them room and kept moving.

Farther in, the crystal itself changed. The columns grew pale and cloudy, veined with a milky white, and along one wall a crust of it had grown over an older marking — a chisel-cut ledge, man-made, its edge now half-swallowed by the mineral growth. Someone had worked this chamber once, before the crystals took it. A rusted iron ring remained set in the stone beside it, the kind used for tethering loads, and the growth had covered it so long ago that the crystal had weathered over the iron itself.

The tracks ran deep and single, and he followed them down the long aisle of glowing columns. The light grew as he went. The crystals burned bluer here, taller, their veins pulsing in that slow breathing rhythm, and the drift of chips underfoot thickened until each step sank past the ankle and whispered and slid. The scraping kept on somewhere off among the ranks — a stroke, a pause, a stroke — but it passed on his left and he passed it by, and neither turned toward the other.

The gallery opened.

The columns ended at a broad bowl of floor, and at its center the glow had a source. A throne of crystal rose there, grown rather than built — a mass of pale blue spars taller than a man, branching upward, every face lit from within, and the light of the whole chamber breathed with it. Around its base the chips lay heaped in drifts higher than his knee.

And on the throne, filling it, sat the queen.

She was the beetle shape grown vast — a shield-backed body the size of a hay wagon, her carapace cut from living crystal, translucent and blue-lit, so that he could see the slow pulse of something inside her where the light moved. Her legs were jointed spars, folded at rest. Her head, low over the heap before her, bore mandibles the length of his forearm, and as he stopped at the last column she was working them over a lump of raw crystal — the scraping, the patient stroke he had followed through half the gallery. She shaved a flake free. It fell glittering. She took it up, and it was gone.

The chamber's breathing light rose and fell with the pulse inside her, and the whole lit bowl of the floor lay between her and him — open ground, blue-shining, with nowhere in it to hide. She had not raised her head.

He did not go far. Among the outermost spars, where the cleft's black slot still showed within reach, he settled his back against a column and let the staff-light die to a coal-glow in his lap, and there he stayed while the gallery's blue breathing rose and fell and rose again.

Two hours is a long time to sit still with a queen. She kept her rhythm the whole while — a stroke, a pause, a flake falling somewhere beyond the ranks of crystal — and he learned the sound the way a shepherd learns a stream, until it stopped meaning danger and meant only that the deep was still itself. Once the scraping broke off. He sat with his hand flat on the cold floor and his breath shallow for the better part of a hundred heartbeats before it picked up again, unhurried, and he let the breath go. Dust settled on his knees, his shoulders, the backs of his hands. His body mended itself slowly in the dark, the sting in his flesh fading to an itch and the itch to nothing, though no rest anywhere called back what the casting had spent; that hollow stayed hollow.

The light did not change. The dust did not stop. Near the end of his two hours a beetle's dry clatter echoed faintly from somewhere down the way he had not gone — the Third Gallery's dark, beyond the throne — distant and brief, and then the gallery's quiet closed over it again.

He rose at last out of the blue glow, joints stiff with sitting, staff in hand, dusted pale to the elbow. The queen's scraping went on, steady as a mill.

messages.mes:
Four more hours he gave the dark.

He made a rough camp of it this time, since it was to be a long sitting — the pack off, his back to the same column, the staff across his knees where one hand could find it without looking. He ate from what he carried, quietly, chewing slow so the sound stayed small, and drank, and settled in to let the hollow inside him fill.

It filled slowly. The mana came back the way water comes back to a well drawn dry — a seep at first, then a steadier rise, and he sat with his eyes half shut and felt the gallery's blue breathing fall into step with it until he could not have said which pulse was the chamber's and which his own. The queen scraped on beyond the ranks. A stroke, a pause, a flake. Twice the rhythm stopped, and twice it resumed, and by the second time he no longer opened his eyes for it.

The Dungeon kept its own hours around him. Dust drifted. Somewhere far off in the Third Gallery a beetle clattered once, faint as a knuckle on a door. The cleft's bright bar lay across the floor, and once — he was not sure, drifting near sleep, and did not go to look — the blue within it seemed to swell a shade brighter before easing back, as if the deep had turned over in its sleep.

By the end he was whole again. The hollow in him stood filled to its walls, and the ache of the casting was a memory only, and his body felt new. He ate a little more, packed, and rose, and rolled his shoulders, and stood a moment at the cleft with the throne-glow washing pale up his face.

It was evening in the world, though no evening reached here. The queen's light did not keep hours. She was still there, still shaving her crystal, still unaware — and the hours had given him back everything but the choice.

messages.mes:
He went back the way he had come, through the Third Gallery and the dark passage beyond the rock shelf, and the grotto let him go. The Second Chamber lay empty, only the pale scatter of spent quartz and the smell of burnt chitin where the fight had been. At the cleft, evening air met him, cool and tasting of grass after the mineral stillness inside, and the stream ran out of the rock beside him, chattering, indifferent.

The road south was empty at that hour. He walked it with his side stiffening, the bite wound throbbing under crusted blood, the venom's heat working itself out slowly as a dull ache rather than anything worse. Light failed over the fields; a cart overtook him near dusk, the carter giving him one long look at his bloodied robes and saying nothing. Glassmere's lamps were already lit when the town wall rose ahead of him, and the watchman at the gate took in the state of him and jerked his thumb through without a word.

The Guild hall was warm and half-full, lamplight on the long counter, a pair of tired-looking adventurers at the far end over mugs. The clerk looked up from her stack of slips as he reached the desk.

"Back late," she said, and then her eyes found the blood. "You sat down or you're bleeding on my floor?"

She had the slip from him all the same, turned it over, and rubbed her thumb across the seal. The READY mark glowed faintly at her touch. She looked at it, then at him, and something in her manner shifted a degree toward interest.

"Glimmerdeep, cleared. Whole outer level." She set the slip down, produced her stamp, and pressed it hard onto the paper. "That'll make the academy happy — they've had field lessons sitting idle a week." She counted the payout out onto the counter, copper in neat stacks. "One hundred and twenty. Count it if you like."

She slid it across and took the slip back for the rolls.

"That's you closed. Anything else, or are you for the healer's?"
